stories.title: HMF Americana Developing Charlotte Mixed-Use Community
stories.excerpt: HMF Americana acquired a development site from Harris Teeter near the border of Stallings and Weddington in Charlotte to build a mixed-use community. The planned development will include 221 rental homes, dedicated 55+ residences, and approximately 10,000 square feet of multi-tenant commercial space. Site work is expected to begin in October, followed by vertical construction in the first quarter of 2027 and initial resident move-ins beginning in the third quarter of 2027. The project combines elements of build-to-rent and multifamily living to create rental communities with the feel of traditional neighborhoods. HMF’s communities feature a mix of cottage-style residences and shared spaces designed around neighborhood connection while providing residents with the convenience of renting. A dedicated portion of the 221-home community will be designed for residents 55 and older. The development will initially feature approximately 10,000 square feet of multi-tenant commercial space, with additional land available for future expansion. The post HMF Americana Developing Charlotte Mixed-Use Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: HMF Americana acquiring Harris Teeter site near Charlotte (Stallings/Weddington border) for 221 rental homes.
Mixed-use project includes 55+ senior housing, 10k SF retail, vertical construction Q1 2027, move-ins Q3 2027.
Build-to-rent cottage-style model with shared spaces; additional commercial land available for expansion.
stories.summary: HMF Americana is developing a 221-unit rental community on a former Harris Teeter site in the Stallings/Weddington submarket south of Charlotte, with 55+ dedicated units and 10,000 SF of commercial space. Site work begins October 2026; vertical construction starts Q1 2027 with initial move-ins in Q3 2027. The project blends cottage-style BTR with traditional neighborhood amenities and mixed-use retail.
stories.impact: This signals strong demand absorption in Charlotte's southern submarkets and confidence in the local rental market. The 55+ component and future commercial expansion potential indicate developers see demographic and mixed-use optionality in secondary Charlotte corridors, suggesting steady rent growth and occupancy tailwinds in that ring despite new supply pipeline.

stories.title: Reforming Pilates to Open New Studio at 233 East 34th Street in Murray Hill
stories.excerpt: Almost started this story with a workout pun, but that would have been too much of a stretch. Fitness brand Reforming Pilates, which offers reformer equipment classes and heated mat workouts, has signed a 10-year, 2,500-square-foot lease to open a new location at 233 East 34th Street, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. “Murray Hill is the heartbeat of Manhattan,” Genevieve Ross, founder of Reforming Pilates, said in a statement. “It’s where you move after college, where you find your people, and where New York really starts to feel like home. It’s young, it’s fun, and it was once my own playground. For me, opening here feels full circle — and I truly believe it’s one of the hottest places to be a brand in the city right now.” The deal represents the studio’s third Manhattan location, following spots at 109 West 17th Street in the Flatiron District and at 1305 Second Avenue on the Upper East Side. The asking rent for this deal was not disclosed, but the average asking rent for retail space in Manhattan’s nearby Herald Square neighborhood was $394 per square foot during the second quarter of 2026, according to CBRE data. The landlord was represented in the deal by Meridian’s Noam Aziz, Carson Shahrabani and Max Freudenberger. “Murray Hill is evolving into a much more health-conscious and wellness-driven customer base,” Freudenberger said in a statement. “There is a growing demand for Pilates, fitness, wellness and health-focused concepts, and we believe this shift is creating a strong opportunity for operators that cater to today’s increasingly health-conscious consumer.” The South Florida-based Reforming Pilates was represented by Jeff Jacobson from Masonre. “We were not looking for another box,” Jacobson said in a statement. “Reforming Pilates needed a ground-floor studio in Murray Hill that could sit next to the Upper East Side and the Flatiron townhouse without dropping the standard — visible, purpose-built, 10 years.” Reforming Pilat
bullets: Reforming Pilates signing 10-year, 2,500 SF lease at 233 East 34th Street, Murray Hill Manhattan.
Third Manhattan location; prior spaces in Flatiron and Upper East Side; brand characterizes Murray Hill as 'hottest places.'
No lease rate disclosed; reflects retail leasing activity in secondary Manhattan submarkets.
stories.summary: Fitness brand Reforming Pilates has leased 2,500 SF for 10 years at 233 East 34th Street in Murray Hill, marking its third Manhattan location. Founder Genevieve Ross cited Murray Hill as a young, vital neighborhood attracting post-college talent and new residents. The deal underscores continued leasing velocity in Manhattan's non-prime retail corridors.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. However, Reforming Pilates' expansion into Murray Hill reflects operator confidence in the neighborhood's younger demographic concentration and rental population stability—a trailing indicator of sustained demand for entry-level and mid-market multifamily in that submarket.

stories.title: Walmart to Build $1.3B Franklin County Fulfillment Center
stories.excerpt: Walmart plans to build a high-tech fulfillment center in Carnesville, creating 1,000 new jobs and bringing $1.3 billion in investment to Franklin County. Carnesville is approximately 85 miles northeast of Atlanta. The new 1.5 million-square-foot automated facility will be located at the Franklin 85 Logistics Center in Carnesville. Walmart’s fulfillment centers are located in strategic markets to expand same-day and next-day shipping capabilities across the United States. Construction is expected to begin in late 2026. From a production standpoint, Walmart operates its new 300,000-square-foot dairy processing facility in Valdosta, Ga., which officially opened late last year. Walmart’s presence in Georgia includes 209 Walmart stores and Sam’s Clubs, as well as 11 supply chain facilities, employing more than 65,300 associates across the state. The retailer also supports local businesses in Georgia, spending more than $26.2 billion with Georgia suppliers and supporting more than 167,600 supplier jobs in fiscal year 2025, alone. The post Walmart to Build $1.3B Franklin County Fulfillment Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Walmart investing $1.3B in 1.5M SF fulfillment center in Carnesville, Franklin County, Georgia (85 miles NE Atlanta).
Project creates 1,000 jobs; construction begins late 2026; augments Walmart's Georgia footprint (209 stores, 11 supply chain facilities, 65k+ employees).
Strategic expansion of same-day/next-day logistics capability; facility complements new Valdosta dairy processing plant.
stories.summary: Walmart is committing $1.3 billion to a 1.5 million-square-foot automated fulfillment center in Carnesville, Franklin County, GA, creating 1,000 jobs with construction beginning late 2026. The investment expands Walmart's logistics network across Georgia and enhances same-day and next-day shipping capabilities. Walmart already operates 209 stores and 11 supply chain facilities in Georgia, employing over 65,300.
stories.impact: Significant demand driver for multifamily development in Franklin County and greater Atlanta exurban markets. The 1,000 direct jobs plus multiplier effect (construction, supporting services, contractors) will attract working-age in-migration to a historically less-dense area, creating a multi-year window for rental housing development ahead of the 2026-2027 absorption wave. Developers should evaluate land/entitlements in Carnesville, Madison, and I-85 corridor submarkets.

stories.title: Tishman Speyer Completes $340M Refinancing of West Loop Office Complex
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer has refinanced The Franklin, a two-tower office complex in Chicago’s West Loop, with a $340 million CMBS loan. The loan was led by JPMorgan with Bank of America and Deutsche Bank serving as co-lenders. Proceeds from the five-year floating rate loan, structured with a two-year initial term and three 12-month extension options, will be used to pay off The Franklin’s existing loan and fund ongoing leasing efforts. Tishman Speyer has secured 460,000 square feet of new leases and extensions at The Franklin since June 2025, bringing the property to 84 percent leased. The Franklin encompasses a 60-story tower at 227 West Monroe Street and a 34-story tower at 222 West Adams Street. The property’s mix of retailers includes Amazon Go, Citibank and Soprafinna Market. “This successful refinancing reflects the strength of The Franklin and the continued demand for premier, amenity-rich workplaces in prime locations,” said Tishman Speyer’s Managing Director Nooshin Felsenthal. bullets: Tishman Speyer refinancing The Franklin (two towers, West Loop Chicago) with $340M CMBS loan led by JPMorgan.

stories.summary: Tishman Speyer has secured a $340 million CMBS refinancing for The Franklin, a two-tower office complex in Chicago's West Loop, led by JPMorgan with BofA and Deutsche Bank as co-lenders. The floating-rate loan has a five-year term (2-year initial plus three 12-month extension options) and will pay off existing debt and fund leasing initiatives. The property has achieved 84% occupancy after securing 460,000 SF of new leases and extensions since June 2025.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. However, refinancing success at 84% occupancy signals modest stabilization in Chicago office, which could reduce conversion-to-residential urgency in the West Loop and slow adaptive-reuse transaction activity—a minor headwind for multifamily developers betting on office-to-residential conversion opportunities in that submarket.

stories.title: Newmark Arranges $215.8M Loan for 5-Property Florida Multifamily Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged $215.8 million in bridge refinancing for Waypoint Residential’s five-property, 1,274-unit multifamily portfolio spanning key markets throughout Florida. Newmark’s Matthew Williams and Rob Wright secured the construction takeout bridge financing through Benefit Street Partners, with support from James Maynard and Kyle Schlitt. The portfolio comprises five newly constructed, luxury garden-style multifamily communities in Vero Beach, Port St. Lucie, Palm Bay, Davenport and Gainesville. Three properties are located along Florida’s Treasure Coast and Space Coast and were completed in 2024, benefiting from continued population and employment growth, a moderating new supply pipeline and proximity to major healthcare, aerospace, advanced manufacturing and logistics employers.  The remaining two properties include The Bradley at Lake Wilson in Davenport (shown), which benefits from access to Orlando’s employment centers, tourism corridor and major transportation infrastructure and The Marlow Gainesville, located near the University of Florida and UF Health, two of the area’s largest economic drivers. The post Newmark Arranges $215.8M Loan for 5-Property Florida Multifamily Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Newmark arranging $215.8M bridge refinancing for Waypoint Residential's five-property, 1,274-unit Florida portfolio.

stories.summary: Newmark arranged $215.8 million in bridge refinancing for Waypoint Residential's five-property, 1,274-unit luxury garden-style multifamily portfolio across key Florida markets. Three newly completed properties (2024) along the Treasure and Space Coasts benefit from population and employment growth and a moderating supply pipeline. The remaining two properties, located in Davenport and Gainesville, provide access to Orlando employment centers and the University of Florida/UF Health ecosystem.
stories.impact: Demonstrates strong capital availability and lender confidence in Florida's multifamily fundamentals, particularly in secondary markets (Vero, Port St. Lucie, Davenport, Gainesville) with secular in-migration and employer anchors. Bridge financing at this scale signals stabilized 2024-built assets command takeout debt, validating development feasibility and rents in Florida's tier-2 markets—a green light for similar projects in healthcare, aerospace, and logistics-adjacent submarkets.

stories.title: Proptech Unicorn EliseAI Launches AI Agent Apollo
stories.excerpt: EliseAI, a leading artificial intelligence company automating housing and health care facilities and one of the first proptech firms to be valued at $1 billion, announced Thursday that it has launched Apollo, its first cross-platform agentic AI tool. A single AI agent capable of performing any task on the Elise platform, Apollo is designed as a new user interface for leasing agents, executives and others in property operations, according to the company. “Apollo is native to our platform, so anything you can do on the Elise AI platform, you can do with Apollo,” said Francesca Loftus, chief experience officer at Manhattan-based EliseAI. “It can execute requests as well as give you access to data across the entire system. A leasing agent would be able to say, ‘Send an updated message for everybody who toured yesterday,’ and be able to provide a message that gets sent out automatically through Apollo across everybody who fits those requirements.” Apollo can also provide next steps based on users’ questions “in plain language, both text and verbal,” Loftus added. Among Apollo’s functions are knowing a customer’s setup, as it understands every setting, permission and data definition specific to a team’s properties. EliseAI said Apollo acts at scale and has been tested against real operations, having run through thousands of tests covering everyday scenarios, from onboarding a new team member to first leasing inquiries, maintenance emergencies, and renewal conversations. It also inherits each user’s existing permissions, so it sees and does only what that person is already cleared for. “Every property team already has a dozen dashboards and reports telling them what happened,” Minna Song, co-founder and CEO of EliseAI, said in a statement. “[Apollo] already knows a team’s data, permissions and priorities well enough that people can ask it a question in plain English, get a real answer back, and see something actually happen because of it
bullets: EliseAI (proptech unicorn, $1B+ valuation) launching Apollo, cross-platform agentic AI tool for property operations.
Apollo enables leasing agents, executives to execute tasks via plain-language voice/text commands across Elise platform.
Automates tenant follow-up, data access, messaging; designed for user interface simplification and operational efficiency.
stories.summary: EliseAI, a proptech unicorn valued at $1 billion-plus, has launched Apollo, an agentic AI tool enabling leasing agents, executives, and property operations staff to execute tasks via plain-language voice or text commands. Apollo integrates natively with the Elise platform and can automate tenant follow-up, provide data access across systems, and trigger workflows such as sending updated messages to recent property tours.
stories.impact: Indirect but meaningful: Apollo's automation of leasing, follow-up, and tenant communication workflows reduces per-unit leasing cost and accelerates lease conversion, improving NOI on stabilized assets. For new developments, faster leasing cycles reduce time-to-stabilization, improve pro forma returns, and free capital for next deals. Wider adoption of such tools will set efficiency benchmarks across the industry, pressuring operators using legacy systems.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Libby McKinney Tritschler of William Raveis Real Estate
stories.excerpt: Community connection plays a huge part in Libby McKinney Tritschler’s approach to clients. McKinney Tritschler, 65, is the executive vice president of sales and the founder of the On The Harbor real estate team at William Raveis Real Estate. She has more than 20 years of experience at the firm and is an expert in Connecticut’s Southport, Fairfield and Westport markets, where she has closed over $800 million in sales. Having grown up in Fairfield County, McKinney Tritschler is involved in many community initiatives in the area, including serving on the board of the Pequot Library, the Westport/Weston YMCA, and the Shepherds Mentors program. Commercial Observer caught up with McKinney Tritschler at the end of August for a series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we connect with residential brokers to learn more about what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career so far? Libby McKinney Tritschler: I’ve had two that really stand out, for very different reasons. The first was 66 Beachside Avenue, a 7-acre parcel on Long Island Sound. The property had been in my family since the mid-1800s and was the last of our family’s waterfront land that had once been part of the Bedford estates. It was an incredibly emotional sale for me because there was so much family history tied to that property. The land traded for $16 million. The other was 260 Willow Street, which I sold at the beginning of 2026 for $12 million. I represented both the seller and the buyer. The seller had moved to Italy, and I was honored to be the person they trusted to oversee everything here, from preparing and managing the property through the entire marketing and sale process. It was an extraordinary responsibility and one I was very proud to have been given. What is your career Everest? Of course, I have financial and sales goals. stories.title: Liability Litigation Is Choking Multifamily Housing
stories.excerpt: Across the U.S., owners of multifamily properties are confronting a growing problem that threatens the health of our housing: The cost and availability of liability insurance is making it increasingly difficult to operate a building. The strain, which threatens to stall much-needed housing development, hits smaller landlords hardest, undercutting cash flow, jeopardizing maintenance budgets, and in some cases putting loans and transactions at risk. While property owners are struggling with cost increases for labor, energy, taxes and financing, liability coverage is the fastest-rising expense. “Nuclear verdicts” (jury awards exceeding $10 million) are a major source of this problem. In 2023, there were 89 nuclear verdicts totaling roughly $14.5 billion in awards. In 2024, those numbers surged to 135 such verdicts, with awards ballooning into the tens of billions. Danielle Lombardo. PHOTO: COurtesy Howden U.S. Real Estate Carriers, reacting to what the market calls “social inflation,” have tightened terms, raised prices, narrowed capacity and, increasingly, carved out or reduced limits for certain high-severity exposures. When payouts become larger and less foreseeable, insurers are compelled to protect capital by withdrawing or constraining coverage. The knock-on effect plays out most directly in lending. Agency guidance, including from major mortgage buyers such as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, now expects general liability and umbrella policies to cover, without exclusion or crippling sublimits, several serious exposures, including assault and battery, firearms, sexual abuse and molestation, and habitability failures. Where those coverages aren’t available, lenders are requiring large escrow accounts or reserves to bridge the gap. Owners have reported that lenders are, in some cases, asking for reserves of $250,000 or more for each excluded exposure. bullets: Multifamily owners facing soaring liability insurance costs and limited availability; fastest-rising expense after labor, energy, taxes.
'Nuclear verdicts' ($10M+) surged from 89 in 2023 ($14.5B total) to 135 in 2024 (tens of billions total awards).

stories.summary: U.S. multifamily owners are confronting escalating liability insurance costs and reduced availability, driven by a surge in 'nuclear verdicts' (jury awards exceeding $10 million). Nuclear verdicts jumped from 89 in 2023 ($14.5 billion total) to 135 in 2024 with awards in the tens of billions. Carriers are tightening terms, raising premiums, reducing capacity, and narrowing coverage, creating a severe cash flow and operational headwind particularly for smaller operators and threatening housing development pipelines.
stories.impact: Significant cost headwind to multifamily development and operations. Rising liability insurance premiums and narrowed coverage reduce operating margins and jeopardize refinance/sale valuations, slowing new construction underwriting. Smaller, undercapitalized developers face reduced feasibility; larger operators with scale and risk management infrastructure gain competitive advantage. Developers should factor 15-25% year-over-year insurance cost escalation into 5-year proformas and consider self-insurance strategies or bundled captive programs.

stories.title: Albany Plans $25M Makeover for Government Complex
stories.excerpt: New York’s Office of General Services (OGS) plans to spend $25 million to improve Empire State Plaza, a 98-acre complex of state government buildings in Albany, with the aim of creating a more active and accessible civic space. Detailed in a report prepared for OGS by architecture and design studio WXY, the plan draws on input from over 2,000 participants and envisions major enhancements to the complex, including green space, improved wayfinding and navigation, upgrades to the visitor experience in the Concourse and the Plaza, and improvements to the Swan Street and Madison Avenue gateways to the Plaza. The investment forms part of the $400 million Championing Albany’s Potential Initiative that Gov. Kathy Hochul launched last year in a bid to promote housing growth, attract new residents, and revitalize public spaces in New York’s capital city. OGS, the state’s real estate arm, oversaw the construction of the Plaza and has served as its caretaker since the complex was completed in 1978. bullets: New York OGS planning $25M investment in Empire State Plaza renovation (98-acre Albany government complex).
Initiative includes green space, wayfinding, Concourse/Plaza upgrades, Swan/Madison Avenue gateway improvements.

stories.summary: New York's Office of General Services (OGS) is allocating $25 million to revitalize Empire State Plaza, a 98-acre government complex in Albany, with improvements to green space, wayfinding, visitor experience, and gateway access. The investment is part of Gov. Hochul's $400 million Championing Albany's Potential Initiative, launched to drive housing growth, attract residents, and revitalize public spaces in New York's capital.
stories.impact: Indirect but meaningful demand signal for Albany multifamily development. State-level investment in civic infrastructure and public space typically precedes private market confidence in housing demand. This signaling, combined with the $400M initiative's explicit housing growth mandate, suggests Albany will see modest population in-migration and rising rents over 3-5 years. Developers should evaluate Albany's downtown and midtown submarkets for mixed-use and rental opportunities ahead of broader revitalization.

stories.title: Westfield Montgomery Owner Pays Off $350M Loan on Bethesda, Md., Mall
stories.excerpt: Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) has paid off a $350 million loan tied to the Westfield Montgomery shopping mall in Bethesda, Md., more than two years after the debt was transferred to special servicing. The 1.2 million-square-foot mall’s loan had been scheduled to mature Aug. 1, Bisnow reported. Morningstar Credit described the payoff as a “rarity in a cycle” in which many mall loans continue to receive extensions. URW secured the 10-year loan in 2014, with the debt tied to 836,000 square feet of the property. The mall received a two-year extension after missing its original August 2024 maturity date. French mall giant URW won approval in 2020 to redevelop Westfield Montgomery, but that project has not started. URW did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The payoff comes as URW has reversed course on its broader U.S. strategy. In 2022, the company said it planned to sell its $13.2 billion American portfolio, but last year opted instead to retain 11 high-performing flagship malls while continuing to unload non-core properties. Meanwhile, Westfield Montgomery has continued adding retailers and restaurants. The mall said in July that new arrivals throughout 2026 would include Pop Mart and Wetzel’s Pretzels, among others. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) paying off $350M loan on Westfield Montgomery (1.2M SF mall, Bethesda, MD).
Loan scheduled maturity August 1; debt had been in special servicing; rare payoff in cycle of extension-heavy mall loans.
URW halted redevelopment plans in 2020; reversed 2022 strategy to sell U.S. portfolio, now retaining 11 flagship malls.
stories.summary: Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield (URW) has paid off a $350 million loan on Westfield Montgomery, a 1.2 million-square-foot mall in Bethesda, Maryland, more than two years after the debt entered special servicing. The payoff is rare in a cycle dominated by mall loan extensions. URW had planned to redevelop the property in 2020 but has not initiated work; the company reversed its 2022 strategy to divest its $13.2 billion U.S. mall portfolio, opting instead to retain 11 high-performing flagships.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily. However, URW's payoff and portfolio pivot toward 'high-performing flagships' suggest cautious optimism on suburban retail but undermine the adaptive-reuse-to-multifamily thesis for secondary malls like Montgomery. Bethesda is a strong renter magnet, but the stalled redevelopment and URW's conservative strategy reduce conversion opportunity urgency in that submarket and extend the life of traditional retail assets.
